This typically leads to denial of service or an information exposure when the application attempts to process the pathname as a regular file.
terms: Improper Handling of Windows Device Names

entries.name: Always-Incorrect Control Flow Implementation
entries.text: The code contains a control flow path that does not reflect the algorithm that the path is intended to implement, leading to incorrect behavior any time this path is navigated.

entries.name: Lack of Administrator Control over Security
entries.text: The product uses security features in a way that prevents the product's administrator from tailoring security settings to reflect the environment in which the product is being used.
terms: Lack of Administrator Control over Security

entries.name: Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release
entries.text: The product uses, accesses, or otherwise operates on a resource after that resource has been expired, released, or revoked.

entries.name: External Influence of Sphere Definition
entries.text: The product does not prevent the definition of control spheres from external actors.

entries.name: Uncontrolled Recursion
entries.text: The product does not properly control the amount of recursion that takes place, consuming excessive resources, such as allocated memory or the program stack.

entries.name: Multiple Operations on Resource in Single-Operation Context
entries.text: The product performs the same operation on a resource two or more times, when the operation should only be applied once.

entries.name: Use of Potentially Dangerous Function
entries.text: The product invokes a potentially dangerous function that could introduce a vulnerability if it is used incorrectly, but the function can also be used safely.

entries.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Overflow
entries.text: The product performs a calculation to determine how much memory to allocate, but an integer overflow can occur that causes less memory to be allocated than expected, leading to a buffer overflow.

entries.name: Incorrect Conversion between Numeric Types
entries.text: When converting from one data type to another, such as long to integer, data can be omitted or translated in a way that produces unexpected values. If the resulting values are used in a sensitive context, then dangerous behaviors may occur.

entries.name: Incorrect Calculation
entries.text: The product performs a calculation that generates incorrect or unintended results that are later used in security-critical decisions or resource management.

entries.name: Function Call With Incorrect Order of Arguments
entries.text: The product calls a function, procedure, or routine, but the caller specifies the arguments in an incorrect order.

entries.name: Incorrect Provision of Specified Functionality
entries.text: The code does not function according to its published specifications, potentially leading to incorrect usage.

entries.name: Function Call With Incorrect Number of Arguments
entries.text: The product calls a function, procedure, or routine, but the caller specifies too many arguments, or too few arguments, which may lead to undefined behavior and resultant weaknesses.

entries.name: Function Call With Incorrect Argument Type
entries.text: The product calls a function, procedure, or routine, but the caller specifies an argument that is the wrong data type, which may lead to resultant weaknesses.
terms: Function Call With Incorrect Argument Type

entries.name: Function Call With Incorrectly Specified Argument Value
entries.text: The product calls a function, procedure, or routine, but the caller specifies an argument that contains the wrong value, which may lead to resultant weaknesses.

entries.name: Function Call With Incorrect Variable or Reference as Argument
entries.text: The product calls a function, procedure, or routine, but the caller specifies the wrong variable or reference as one of the arguments, which may lead to undefined behavior and resultant weaknesses.

entries.name: Permission Race Condition During Resource Copy
entries.text: The product, while copying or cloning a resource, does not set the resource's permissions or access control until the copy is complete, leaving the resource exposed to other spheres while the copy is taking place.
terms: Permission Race Condition During Resource Copy

entries.name: Improper Handling of Windows ::DATA Alternate Data Stream
entries.text: The product does not properly prevent access to, or detect usage of, alternate data streams (ADS).

entries.name: Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference
entries.text: The product does not check for an error after calling a function that can return with a NULL pointer if the function fails, which leads to a resultant NULL pointer dereference.

entries.name: Insufficient Control Flow Management
entries.text: The code does not sufficiently manage its control flow during execution, creating conditions in which the control flow can be modified in unexpected ways.

entries.name: Incomplete Denylist to Cross-Site Scripting
entries.text: The product uses a denylist-based protection mechanism to defend against XSS attacks, but the denylist is incomplete.

entries.name: Protection Mechanism Failure
entries.text: The product does not use or incorrectly uses a protection mechanism that provides sufficient defense against directed attacks against the product.

entries.name: Use of Multiple Resources with Duplicate Identifier
entries.text: The product uses multiple resources that can have the same identifier, in a context in which unique identifiers are required.

entries.name: Use of Low-Level Functionality
entries.text: The product uses low-level functionality that is explicitly prohibited by the framework or specification under which the product is supposed to operate.

entries.name: Incorrect Behavior Order
entries.text: The product performs multiple related behaviors, but the behaviors are performed in the wrong order in ways that may produce resultant weaknesses.

entries.name: Incorrect Comparison
entries.text: The product compares two entities in a security-relevant context, but the comparison is incorrect.

entries.name: Execution After Redirect (EAR)
entries.text: The web application sends a redirect to another location, but instead of exiting, it executes additional code.

entries.name: J2EE Misconfiguration: Missing Custom Error Page
entries.text: The product has a J2EE component that does not have a custom error page.
terms: J2EE Misconfiguration: Missing Custom Error Page

entries.name: Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions
entries.text: The product does not properly anticipate or handle exceptional conditions that rarely occur during normal operation of the product.

entries.name: Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast
entries.text: The product does not correctly convert an object, resource, or structure from one type to a different type.

entries.name: Incorrect Control Flow Scoping
entries.text: The product does not properly return control flow to the proper location after it has completed a task or detected an unusual condition.

entries.name: Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference
entries.text: The product uses a name or reference to access a resource, but the name/reference resolves to a resource that is outside of the intended control sphere.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization
entries.text: The product does not ensure or incorrectly ensures that structured messages or data are well-formed and that certain security properties are met before being used when received from an upstream component, or before being sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: Incorrect Ownership Assignment
entries.text: The product assigns an owner to a resource, but the owner is outside of the intended control sphere.

entries.name: Improper Adherence to Coding Standards
entries.text: The product does not follow certain coding rules for development.

entries.name: Improper Handling of Apple HFS+ Alternate Data Stream Path
entries.text: The product does not properly handle special paths that may identify the data or resource fork of a file on the HFS+ file system.

entries.name: External Control of File Name or Path
entries.text: The product allows user input to control or influence paths or file names that are used in filesystem operations.

entries.name: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
entries.text: The product specifies permissions for a security-critical resource in a way that allows that resource to be read or modified by unintended actors.
terms: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

entries.name: Compiler Optimization Removal or Modification of Security-critical Code
entries.text: The developer builds a security-critical protection mechanism into the software, but the compiler optimizes the program such that the mechanism is removed or modified.

entries.name: Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of a command, data structure, or record using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify how it is parsed or interpreted when it is sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: Exposed Dangerous Method or Function
entries.text: The product provides an Applications Programming Interface (API) or similar interface for interaction with external actors, but the interface includes a dangerous method or function that is not properly restricted.

entries.name: Special Element Injection
entries.title: Failure to Sanitize Special Elements into a Different Plane
entries.text: The product does not adequately filter user-controlled input for special elements with control implications.

entries.name: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions
entries.text: The product does not check or incorrectly checks for unusual or exceptional conditions that are not expected to occur frequently during day to day operation of the product.

entries.name: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions
entries.text: The product does not handle or incorrectly handles an exceptional condition.

entries.name: Missing Custom Error Page
entries.text: The product does not return custom error pages to the user, possibly exposing sensitive information.

entries.name: Algorithm Downgrade
entries.title: Selection of Less-Secure Algorithm During Negotiation
entries.text: A protocol or its implementation supports interaction between multiple actors and allows those actors to negotiate which algorithm should be used in a protection mechanism such as encryption or authentication, but it does not select the strongest algorithm that is available to both parties.

entries.name: Reliance on Undefined, Unspecified, or Implementation-Defined Behavior
entries.text: The product uses an API function, data structure, or other entity in a way that relies on properties that are not always guaranteed to hold for that entity.

entries.name: Use of a One-Way Hash without a Salt
entries.text: The product uses a one-way cryptographic hash against an input that should not be reversible, such as a password, but the product does not also use a salt as part of the input.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Equivalent Special Elements
entries.text: The product correctly neutralizes certain special elements, but it improperly neutralizes equivalent special elements.
terms: Improper Neutralization of Equivalent Special Elements

entries.name: Use of a One-Way Hash with a Predictable Salt
entries.text: The product uses a one-way cryptographic hash against an input that should not be reversible, such as a password, but the product uses a predictable salt as part of the input.

entries.name: Free of Pointer not at Start of Buffer
entries.text: The product calls free() on a pointer to a memory resource that was allocated on the heap, but the pointer is not at the start of the buffer.

entries.name: Mismatched Memory Management Routines
entries.text: The product attempts to return a memory resource to the system, but it calls a release function that is not compatible with the function that was originally used to allocate that resource.

entries.name: Release of Invalid Pointer or Reference
entries.text: The product attempts to return a memory resource to the system, but it calls the wrong release function or calls the appropriate release function incorrectly.
terms: Release of Invalid Pointer or Reference

entries.name: Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource
entries.text: The product locks a critical resource more times than intended, leading to an unexpected state in the system.
terms: Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource

entries.name: Multiple Unlocks of a Critical Resource
entries.text: The product unlocks a critical resource more times than intended, leading to an unexpected state in the system.
terms: Multiple Unlocks of a Critical Resource

entries.name: Critical Data Element Declared Public
entries.text: The product declares a critical variable, field, or member to be public when intended security policy requires it to be private.

entries.name: Access to Critical Private Variable via Public Method
entries.text: The product defines a public method that reads or modifies a private variable.

entries.name: Incorrect Short Circuit Evaluation
entries.text: The product contains a conditional statement with multiple logical expressions in which one of the non-leading expressions may produce side effects.

entries.name: Command injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of a command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended command when it is sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
entries.text: The product allocates a reusable resource or group of resources on behalf of an actor without imposing any intended restrictions on the size or number of resources that can be allocated.

entries.name: Missing Reference to Active Allocated Resource
entries.text: The product does not properly maintain a reference to a resource that has been allocated, which prevents the resource from being reclaimed.
terms: Missing Reference to Active Allocated Resource

entries.name: Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime
entries.text: The product does not release a resource after its effective lifetime has ended, i.e., after the resource is no longer needed.

entries.name: Missing Reference to Active File Descriptor or Handle
entries.text: The product does not properly maintain references to a file descriptor or handle, which prevents that file descriptor/handle from being reclaimed.

entries.name: File Descriptor Exhaustion
entries.title: Allocation of File Descriptors or Handles Without Limits or Throttling
entries.text: The product allocates file descriptors or handles on behalf of an actor without imposing any restrictions on how many descriptors can be allocated, in violation of the intended security policy for that actor.

entries.name: Missing Release of File Descriptor or Handle after Effective Lifetime
entries.text: The product does not release a file descriptor or handle after its effective lifetime has ended, i.e., after the file descriptor/handle is no longer needed.

entries.name: Billion Laughs Attack
entries.title: Improper Restriction of Recursive Entity References in DTDs
entries.text: The product uses XML documents and allows their structure to be defined with a Document Type Definition (DTD), but it does not properly control the number of recursive definitions of entities.

entries.name: Regular Expression without Anchors
entries.text: The product uses a regular expression to perform neutralization, but the regular expression omits one or more anchors that may allow malicious or malformed data to slip through.

entries.name: Insufficient Logging
entries.text: When a security-critical event occurs, the product either does not record the event or omits important details about the event when logging it.

entries.name: Logging of Excessive Data
entries.text: The product logs too much information, making log files hard to process and possibly hindering recovery efforts or forensic analysis after an attack.

entries.name: OS Command Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of an OS command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended OS command before it is sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: Use of RSA Algorithm without OAEP
entries.text: The product uses the RSA algorithm but does not incorporate Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (OAEP).
terms: Use of RSA Algorithm without OAEP

entries.name: Improper Address Validation in IOCTL with METHOD_NEITHER I/O Control Code
entries.text: The product defines an IOCTL that uses METHOD_NEITHER for I/O, but it does not validate or incorrectly validates the addresses that are provided.

entries.name: Exposed IOCTL with Insufficient Access Control
entries.text: The product implements an IOCTL with functionality that should be restricted, but it does not properly enforce access control for the IOCTL.
terms: Exposed IOCTL with Insufficient Access Control

entries.name: Operator Precedence Logic Error
entries.text: The product uses an expression in which operator precedence causes incorrect logic to be used.

entries.name: Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking in a Security Decision
entries.text: The product uses a protection mechanism that relies on the existence or values of a cookie, but it does not properly ensure that the cookie is valid for the associated user.

entries.name: Use of Path Manipulation Function without Maximum-sized Buffer
entries.text: The product invokes a function for normalizing paths or file names, but it provides an output buffer that is smaller than the maximum possible size, such as PATH_MAX.

entries.name: Access of Memory Location Before Start of Buffer
entries.text: The product reads or writes to a buffer using an index or pointer that references a memory location prior to the beginning of the buffer.

entries.name: Out-of-bounds Write
entries.text: The product writes data past the end, or before the beginning, of the intended buffer.

entries.name: Access of Memory Location After End of Buffer
entries.text: The product reads or writes to a buffer using an index or pointer that references a memory location after the end of the buffer.

entries.name: Stack Exhaustion
entries.title: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value
entries.text: The product allocates memory based on an untrusted, large size value, but it does not ensure that the size is within expected limits, allowing arbitrary amounts of memory to be allocated.
terms: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value

entries.name: Cross-site Scripting
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
entries.text: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input before it is placed in output that is used as a web page that is served to other users.

entries.name: Improper Filtering of Special Elements
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but it does not filter or incorrectly filters special elements before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Incomplete Filtering of Special Elements
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but it does not completely filter special elements before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Incomplete Filtering of One or More Instances of Special Elements
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but does not completely filter one or more instances of special elements before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Only Filtering One Instance of a Special Element
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but only filters a single instance of a special element before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Incomplete Filtering of Multiple Instances of Special Elements
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but it does not filter all instances of a special element before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Only Filtering Special Elements at a Specified Location
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but only accounts for special elements at a specified location, thereby missing remaining special elements that may exist before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Only Filtering Special Elements Relative to a Marker
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but only accounts for special elements positioned relative to a marker (e.g. "at the beginning/end of a string; the second argument"), thereby missing remaining special elements that may exist before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Only Filtering Special Elements at an Absolute Position
entries.text: The product receives data from an upstream component, but only accounts for special elements at an absolute position (e.g. "byte number 10"), thereby missing remaining special elements that may exist before sending it to a downstream component.

entries.name: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
entries.text: The product contains hard-coded credentials, such as a password or cryptographic key.

entries.name: Improper Control of Interaction Frequency
entries.text: The product does not properly limit the number or frequency of interactions that it has with an actor, such as the number of incoming requests.

entries.name: J2EE Misconfiguration: Entity Bean Declared Remote
entries.text: The J2EE application exposes a remote interface for an entity bean, but it also exposes methods that get or set the bean's data.
terms: J2EE Misconfiguration: Entity Bean Declared Remote

entries.name: Basic XSS
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags in a Web Page
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special characters such as "", and "&" that could be interpreted as web-scripting elements when they are sent to a downstream component that processes web pages.

entries.name: Guessable CAPTCHA
entries.text: The product uses a CAPTCHA challenge, but the challenge can be guessed or automatically recognized by a non-human actor.

entries.name: Buffer Access with Incorrect Length Value
entries.text: The product uses a sequential operation to read or write a buffer, but it uses an incorrect length value that causes it to access memory that is outside of the bounds of the buffer.
terms: Buffer Access with Incorrect Length Value

entries.name: Buffer Access Using Size of Source Buffer
entries.text: The product uses the size of a source buffer when reading from or writing to a destination buffer, which may cause it to access memory that is outside of the bounds of the buffer.

entries.name: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
entries.text: The product uses a protection mechanism that relies on the existence or values of an input, but the input can be modified by an untrusted actor in a way that bypasses the protection mechanism.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Script in an Error Message Web Page
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special characters that could be interpreted as web-scripting elements when they are sent to an error page.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Script in Attributes of IMG Tags in a Web Page
entries.text: The web application does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes scripting elements within attributes of HTML IMG tags, such as the src attribute.

entries.name: Missing Synchronization
entries.text: The product utilizes a shared resource in a concurrent manner but does not attempt to synchronize access to the resource.

entries.name: Incorrect Synchronization
entries.text: The product utilizes a shared resource in a concurrent manner, but it does not correctly synchronize access to the resource.

entries.name: Untrusted Pointer Dereference
entries.text: The product obtains a value from an untrusted source, converts this value to a pointer, and dereferences the resulting pointer.

entries.name: Use of Out-of-range Pointer Offset
entries.text: The product performs pointer arithmetic on a valid pointer, but it uses an offset that can point outside of the intended range of valid memory locations for the resulting pointer.

entries.name: Access of Uninitialized Pointer
entries.text: The product accesses or uses a pointer that has not been initialized.

entries.name: Expired Pointer Dereference
entries.text: The product dereferences a pointer that contains a location for memory that was previously valid, but is no longer valid.

entries.name: Premature Release of Resource During Expected Lifetime
entries.text: The product releases a resource that is still intended to be used by itself or another actor.

entries.name: Improper Control of Document Type Definition
entries.text: The product does not restrict a reference to a Document Type Definition (DTD) to the intended control sphere. This might allow attackers to reference arbitrary DTDs, possibly causing the product to expose files, consume excessive system resources, or execute arbitrary http requests on behalf of the attacker.
terms: Improper Control of Document Type Definition

entries.name: Signal Handler with Functionality that is not Asynchronous-Safe
entries.text: The product defines a signal handler that contains code sequences that are not asynchronous-safe, i.e., the functionality is not reentrant, or it can be interrupted.

entries.name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
entries.text: The product imports, requires, or includes executable functionality (such as a library) from a source that is outside of the intended control sphere.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Script in Attributes in a Web Page
entries.text: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes "javascript:" or other URIs from dangerous attributes within tags, such as onmouseover, onload, onerror, or style.

entries.name: Inclusion of Web Functionality from an Untrusted Source
entries.text: The product includes web functionality (such as a web widget) from another domain in a way that causes the functionality to operate within the domain of the product, potentially granting total access and control of the product to the untrusted source.

entries.name: Signal Handler Function Associated with Multiple Signals
entries.text: The product defines a function that is used as a handler for more than one signal.

entries.name: Unlock of a Resource that is not Locked
entries.text: The product attempts to unlock a resource that is not locked.

entries.name: Deadlock
entries.text: The product contains multiple threads or executable segments that are waiting for each other to release a necessary lock, resulting in deadlock.

entries.name: Excessive Iteration
entries.text: The product performs an iteration or loop without sufficiently limiting the number of times that the loop is executed.

entries.name: Infinite Loop
entries.title: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition
entries.text: The product contains an iteration or loop with an exit condition that cannot be reached, i.e., an infinite loop.

entries.name: Use of Password Hash Instead of Password for Authentication
entries.text: The product includes a client that computes a hash of a password and sends the hash to another component, which compares the supplied hash to the hash obtained from a data store of password hashes.

entries.name: Improper Enforcement of a Single, Unique Action
entries.text: The product requires that an actor should only be able to perform an action once, or to have only one unique action, but the product does not enforce or incorrectly enforces this restriction.

entries.name: Inappropriate Encoding for Output Context
entries.text: The product uses or specifies an encoding when generating output to a downstream component, but the specified encoding is not the same as the encoding that is expected by the downstream component.

entries.name: Signed comparison
entries.title: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check
entries.text: The product checks a value to ensure that it is less than or equal to a maximum, but it does not also verify that the value is greater than or equal to the minimum.
terms: Numeric Range Comparison Without Minimum Check

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page
entries.text: The web application improperly neutralizes user-controlled input for executable script disguised with URI encodings.

entries.name: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow
entries.text: The product supports a session in which more than one behavior must be performed by an actor, but it does not properly ensure that the actor performs the behaviors in the required sequence or timeframe.

entries.name: Placement of User into Incorrect Group
entries.text: The product or the administrator places a user into an incorrect group.
terms: Placement of User into Incorrect Group

entries.name: Type Confusion
entries.title: Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type
entries.text: The product allocates or initializes a resource such as a pointer, object, or variable using one type, but it later accesses that resource using a type that is incompatible with the original type.
terms: Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type

entries.name: Doubled Character XSS Manipulations
entries.text: The web application does not filter user-controlled input for executable script disguised using doubling of the involved characters.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Invalid Characters in Identifiers in Web Pages
entries.text: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes invalid characters or byte sequences in the middle of tag names, URI schemes, and other identifiers.

entries.name: Missing Authorization
entries.text: The product does not perform an authorization check when an actor attempts to access a resource or perform an action.

entries.name: Incorrect Authorization
entries.text: The product performs an authorization check when an actor attempts to access a resource or perform an action, but it does not correctly perform the check.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Alternate XSS Syntax
entries.text: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controlled input for alternate script syntax.
terms: Improper Neutralization of Alternate XSS Syntax

entries.name: Argument Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command
entries.text: The product constructs a string for a command to be executed by a separate component in another control sphere, but it does not properly delimit the intended arguments, options, or switches within that command string.

entries.name: SQL Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: J2EE Misconfiguration: Weak Access Permissions for EJB Methods
entries.text: If elevated access rights are assigned to EJB methods, then an attacker can take advantage of the permissions to exploit the product.

entries.name: LDAP Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an LDAP Query
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of an LDAP query using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended LDAP query when it is sent to a downstream component.

entries.name: Use of Uninitialized Resource
entries.text: The product uses or accesses a resource that has not been initialized.

entries.name: Missing Initialization of Resource
entries.text: The product does not initialize a critical resource.

entries.name: XML Injection
entries.text: The product does not properly neutralize special elements that are used in XML, allowing attackers to modify the syntax, content, or commands of the XML before it is processed by an end system.

entries.name: Use of Expired File Descriptor
entries.text: The product uses or accesses a file descriptor after it has been closed.

entries.name: Improper Update of Reference Count
entries.text: The product uses a reference count to manage a resource, but it does not update or incorrectly updates the reference count.

entries.name: Hidden Functionality
entries.text: The product contains functionality that is not documented, not part of the specification, and not accessible through an interface or command sequence that is obvious to the product's users or administrators.

entries.name: Improper Control of Dynamically-Managed Code Resources
entries.text: The product does not properly restrict reading from or writing to dynamically-managed code resources such as variables, objects, classes, attributes, functions, or executable instructions or statements.

entries.name: Improper Control of Dynamically-Identified Variables
entries.text: The product does not properly restrict reading from or writing to dynamically-identified variables.

entries.name: Mass Assignment
entries.title: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component that specifies multiple attributes, properties, or fields that are to be initialized or updated in an object, but it does not properly control which attributes can be modified.

entries.name: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
entries.text: The product generates a hash for a password, but it uses a scheme that does not provide a sufficient level of computational effort that would make password cracking attacks infeasible or expensive.

entries.name: Expression Language Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of an expression language (EL) statement in a framework such as a Java Server Page (JSP) using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended EL statement before it is executed.

entries.name: Server-Side Request Forgery
entries.text: The web server receives a URL or similar request from an upstream component and retrieves the contents of this URL, but it does not sufficiently ensure that the request is being sent to the expected destination.

entries.name: Improper Restriction of Power Consumption
entries.text: The product operates in an environment in which power is a limited resource that cannot be automatically replenished - or has financial restrictions - but the product does not properly restrict the amount of power that its operation consumes.

entries.name: Storage of Sensitive Data in a Mechanism without Access Control
entries.text: The product stores sensitive information in a file system or device that does not have built-in access control.

entries.name: Insecure Storage of Sensitive Information
entries.text: The product stores sensitive information without properly limiting read or write access by unauthorized actors.

entries.name: Improper Restriction of Communication Channel to Intended Endpoints
entries.text: The product establishes a communication channel to (or from) an endpoint for privileged or protected operations, but it does not properly ensure that it is communicating with the correct endpoint.

entries.name: Improper Enforcement of Message Integrity During Transmission in a Communication Channel
entries.text: The product establishes a communication channel with an endpoint and receives a message from that endpoint, but it does not sufficiently ensure that the message was not modified during transmission.

entries.name: Intent Spoofing
entries.title: Improper Verification of Intent by Broadcast Receiver
entries.text: The Android application uses a Broadcast Receiver that receives an Intent but does not properly verify that the Intent came from an authorized source.

entries.name: Improper Export of Android Application Components
entries.text: The Android application exports a component for use by other applications, but does not properly restrict which applications can launch the component or access the data it contains.
terms: Improper Export of Android Application Components

entries.name: Use of Implicit Intent for Sensitive Communication
entries.text: The Android application uses an implicit intent for transmitting sensitive data to other applications.

entries.name: CRLF Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences
entries.text: The product uses CRLF (carriage return line feeds) as a special element, e.g. to separate lines or records, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes CRLF sequences from inputs.

entries.name: Improper Authorization in Handler for Custom URL Scheme
entries.text: The product uses a handler for a custom URL scheme, but it does not properly restrict which actors can invoke the handler using the scheme.

entries.name: Code Injection
entries.title: Improper Control of Generation of Code
entries.text: The product constructs all or part of a code segment using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the syntax or behavior of the intended code segment.
terms: Improper Control of Generation of Code

entries.name: Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel
entries.text: The product establishes a communication channel to handle an incoming request that has been initiated by an actor, but it does not properly verify that the request is coming from the expected origin.

entries.name: Incorrectly Specified Destination in a Communication Channel
entries.text: The product creates a communication channel to initiate an outgoing request to an actor, but it does not correctly specify the intended destination for that actor.

entries.name: Permissive Cross-domain Security Policy with Untrusted Domains
entries.text: The product uses a web-client protection mechanism such as a Content Security Policy (CSP) or cross-domain policy file, but the policy includes untrusted domains with which the web client is allowed to communicate.

entries.name: NoSQL Injection, NoSQLi
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic
entries.text: The product generates a query intended to access or manipulate data in a data store such as a database, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that can modify the intended logic of the query.

entries.name: Eval Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes code syntax before using the input in a dynamic evaluation call (e.g. "eval").

entries.name: Static Code Injection
entries.title: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Statically Saved Code
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes code syntax before inserting the input into an executable resource, such as a library, configuration file, or template.

entries.name: Improper Neutralization of Server-Side Includes (SSI) Within a Web Page
entries.text: The product generates a web page, but does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input that could be interpreted as a server-side include (SSI) directive.

entries.name: Remote file include
entries.title: Improper Control of Filename for Include/Require Statement in PHP Program
entries.text: The PHP application receives input from an upstream component, but it does not restrict or incorrectly restricts the input before its usage in "require," "include," or similar functions.

entries.name: Resource Injection
entries.title: Improper Control of Resource Identifiers
entries.text: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not restrict or incorrectly restricts the input before it is used as an identifier for a resource that may be outside the intended control sphere.

entries.name: Data Obfuscation
entries.text: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen.

entries.name: Junk Data
entries.text: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult. By adding random or meaningless data to the protocols used for command and control, adversaries can prevent trivial methods for decoding, deciphering, or otherwise analyzing the traffic. Examples may include appending/prepending data with junk characters or writing junk characters between significant characters.

entries.name: Steganography
entries.text: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital messages that are transferred between systems. This hidden information can be used for command and control of compromised systems.

entries.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
entries.text: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts. By impersonating legitimate protocols or web services, adversaries can make their command and control traffic blend in with legitimate network traffic.

entries.name: OS Credential Dumping
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures. Credentials can then be used to perform Lateral Movement and access restricted information.

entries.name: LSASS Memory
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct Lateral Movement using Use Alternate Authentication Material.

entries.name: Security Account Manager
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored. The SAM is a database file that contains local accounts for the host, typically those found with the net user command. Enumerating the SAM database requires SYSTEM level access.

entries.name: NTDS
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights. By default, the NTDS file (NTDS.dit) is located in %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit of a domain controller.

entries.name: LSA Secrets
entries.text: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts. LSA secrets are stored in the registry at HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets. LSA secrets can also be dumped from memory.

entries.name: Cached Domain Credentials
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

entries.name: DCSync
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

entries.name: Proc Filesystem
entries.text: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or `/proc`. The proc filesystem is a pseudo-filesystem used as an interface to kernel data structures for Linux based systems managing virtual memory. For each process, the `/proc//maps` file shows how memory is mapped within the process’s virtual address space.

entries.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking. Most modern Linux operating systems use a combination of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to store user account information, including password hashes in /etc/shadow. By default, /etc/shadow is only readable by the root user.

entries.name: Data from Local System
entries.text: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

entries.name: Direct Volume Access
entries.text: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring. Windows allows programs to have direct access to logical volumes. Programs with direct access may read and write files directly from the drive by analyzing file system data structures. This technique may bypass Windows file access controls as well as file system monitoring tools.

entries.name: System Service Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services. Adversaries may obtain information about services using tools as well as OS utility commands such as sc query, tasklist /svc, systemctl --type=service, and net start. Adversaries may also gather information about schedule tasks via commands such as `schtasks` on Windows or `crontab -l` on Linux and macOS.

entries.name: Fallback Channels
entries.text: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

entries.name: Application Window Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows. Window listings could convey information about how the system is used. For example, information about application windows could be used to identify potential data to collect as well as identifying security tooling (Security Software Discovery) to evade.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, the exfiltration may occur, for example, over a WiFi connection, modem, cellular data connection, Bluetooth, or another radio frequency (RF) channel.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, an adversary may opt to exfiltrate data using a Bluetooth communication channel.

entries.name: Query Registry
entries.text: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

entries.name: Rootkit
entries.text: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components. Rootkits are programs that hide the existence of malware by intercepting/hooking and modifying operating system API calls that supply system information.

entries.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems. Several operating system administration utilities exist that can be used to gather this information. Examples include Arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route.

entries.name: Internet Connection Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. This may be performed during automated discovery and can be accomplished in numerous ways such as using Ping, tracert, and GET requests to websites, or performing initial speed testing to confirm bandwidth.

entries.name: Wi-Fi Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems. Adversaries may use Wi-Fi information as part of Account Discovery, Remote System Discovery, and other discovery or Credential Access activity to support both ongoing and future campaigns.

entries.name: Remote System Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system. Functionality could exist within remote access tools to enable this, but utilities available on the operating system could also be used such as Ping, net view using Net, or, on ESXi servers, `esxcli network diag ping`.

entries.name: Automated Exfiltration
entries.text: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

entries.name: Traffic Duplication
entries.text: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure. Traffic mirroring is a native feature for some devices, often used for network analysis. For example, devices may be configured to forward network traffic to one or more destinations for analysis by a network analyzer or other monitoring device.

entries.name: Remote Services
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: Distributed Component Object Model
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: SSH
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: VNC
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC). VNC is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB (“remote framebuffer”) protocol to enable users to remotely control another computer’s display by relaying the screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs over the network.

entries.name: Windows Remote Management
entries.text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

entries.name: Cloud Services
entries.text: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities. The adversary may then perform management actions or access cloud-hosted resources as the logged-on user.

entries.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
entries.text: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the Cloud API, such as Azure Serial Console, AWS EC2 Instance Connect, and AWS System Manager..

entries.name: Data from Removable Media
entries.text: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest. Sensitive data can be collected from any removable media (optical disk drive, USB memory, etc.) connected to the compromised system prior to Exfiltration. Interactive command shells may be in use, and common functionality within cmd may be used to gather information.

entries.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses.

entries.name: Binary Padding
entries.text: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware. This can be done without affecting the functionality or behavior of a binary, but can increase the size of the binary beyond what some security tools are capable of handling due to file size limitations.

entries.name: Software Packing
entries.text: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable. Packing an executable changes the file signature in an attempt to avoid signature-based detection. Most decompression techniques decompress the executable code in memory.

entries.name: Steganography
entries.text: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files.

entries.name: Compile After Delivery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe, csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.

entries.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
entries.text: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed. They can modify the tool by removing the indicator and using the updated version that is no longer detected by the target's defensive systems or subsequent targets that may use similar systems.

entries.name: HTML Smuggling
entries.text: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files. HTML documents can store large binary objects known as JavaScript Blobs (immutable data that represents raw bytes) that can later be constructed into file-like objects. Data may also be stored in Data URLs, which enable embedding media type or MIME files inline of HTML documents.

entries.name: Dynamic API Resolution
entries.text: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis. Malware commonly uses various Native API functions provided by the OS to perform various tasks such as those involving processes, files, and other system artifacts.

entries.name: Stripped Payloads
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information. Scripts and executables may contain variable names and other strings that help developers document code functionality. Symbols are often created by an operating system’s `linker` when executable payloads are compiled.

entries.name: Embedded Payloads
entries.text: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to Subvert Trust Controls by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.

entries.name: Command Obfuscation
entries.text: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection. Command-line obfuscation is a method of making strings and patterns within commands and scripts more difficult to signature and analyze. This type of obfuscation can be included within commands executed by delivered payloads (e.g., Phishing and Drive-by Compromise) or interactively via Command and Scripting Interpreter.

entries.name: Fileless Storage
entries.text: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.

entries.name: LNK Icon Smuggling
entries.text: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files. Windows shortcut files (.LNK) include many metadata fields, including an icon location field (also known as the `IconEnvironmentDataBlock`) designed to specify the path to an icon file that is to be displayed for the LNK file within a host directory.

entries.name: Encrypted/Encoded File
entries.text: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection. Encrypting and/or encoding file content aims to conceal malicious artifacts within a file used in an intrusion. Many other techniques, such as Software Packing, Steganography, and Embedded Payloads, share this same broad objective.

entries.name: Polymorphic Code
entries.text: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection. Polymorphic code is a type of software capable of changing its runtime footprint during code execution. With each execution of the software, the code is mutated into a different version of itself that achieves the same purpose or objective as the original.

entries.name: Compression
entries.text: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., Fileless Storage).

entries.name: Junk Code Insertion
entries.text: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware’s functionality. Junk code is code that either does not execute, or if it does execute, does not change the functionality of the code. Junk code makes analysis more difficult and time-consuming, as the analyst steps through non-functional code instead of analyzing the main code.

entries.name: SVG Smuggling
entries.text: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files. SVGs, or Scalable Vector Graphics, are vector-based image files constructed using XML. As such, they can legitimately include `` tags that enable adversaries to include malicious JavaScript payloads.

entries.name: Invisible Unicode
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text. By inserting characters that do not visibly render, adversaries may hide data, alter how content is interpreted, or make malicious code appear as benign text or whitespace.

entries.name: Scheduled Transfer
entries.text: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals. This could be done to blend traffic patterns with normal activity or availability.

entries.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
entries.text: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds. This approach may be used to avoid triggering network data transfer threshold alerts.

entries.name: System Owner/User Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system. They may do this, for example, by retrieving account usernames or by using OS Credential Dumping.

entries.name: Masquerading
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation.

entries.name: Invalid Code Signature
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool. Code signing provides a level of authenticity on a binary from the developer and a guarantee that the binary has not been tampered with. Adversaries can copy the metadata and signature information from a signed program, then use it as a template for an unsigned program.

entries.name: Right-to-Left Override
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign. RTLO is a non-printing Unicode character that causes the text that follows it to be displayed in reverse. For example, a Windows screensaver executable named March 25 \u202Excod.scr will display as March 25 rcs.docx.

entries.name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
entries.text: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities. Security monitoring and control mechanisms may be in place for legitimate utilities adversaries are capable of abusing, including both built-in binaries and tools such as PSExec, AutoHotKey, and IronPython.

entries.name: Masquerade Task or Service
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign. Tasks/services executed by the Task Scheduler or systemd will typically be given a name and/or description. Windows services will have a service name as well as a display name. Many benign tasks and services exist that have commonly associated names.

entries.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
entries.text: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them. This is done for the sake of evading defenses and observation.
terms: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

entries.name: Space after Filename
entries.text: Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file. With certain file types (specifically this does not work with .app extensions), appending a space to the end of a filename will change how the file is processed by the operating system.

entries.name: Double File Extension
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type. A file name may include a secondary file type extension that may cause only the first extension to be displayed (ex: File.txt.exe may render in some views as just File.txt). However, the second extension is the true file type that determines how the file is opened and executed.

entries.name: Masquerade File Type
entries.text: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file’s signature, extension, icon, and contents. Various file types have a typical standard format, including how they are encoded and organized.

entries.name: Break Process Trees
entries.text: An adversary may attempt to evade process tree-based analysis by modifying executed malware's parent process ID (PPID). If endpoint protection software leverages the “parent-child" relationship for detection, breaking this relationship could result in the adversary’s behavior not being associated with previous process tree activity.

entries.name: Masquerade Account Name
entries.text: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign. This will typically occur during Create Account, although accounts may also be renamed at a later date. This may also coincide with Account Access Removal if the actor first deletes an account before re-creating one with the same name.

entries.name: Overwrite Process Arguments
entries.text: Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process. On Linux, the operating system stores command-line arguments in the process’s stack and passes them to the `main()` function as the `argv` array.

entries.name: Browser Fingerprint
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc. The HTTP User-Agent request header is a string that lets servers and network peers identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent.

entries.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
entries.text: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence. Initialization scripts can be used to perform administrative functions, which may often execute other programs or send information to an internal logging server. These scripts can vary based on operating system and whether applied locally or remotely.

entries.name: Logon Script (Windows)
entries.text: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Windows allows logon scripts to be run whenever a specific user or group of users log into a system. This is done via adding a path to a script to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key.

entries.name: Login Hook
entries.text: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon. A login hook is a plist file that points to a specific script to execute with root privileges upon user logon. The plist file is located in the /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist file and can be modified using the defaults command-line utility.

entries.name: Network Logon Script
entries.text: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence. Network logon scripts can be assigned using Active Directory or Group Policy Objects. These logon scripts run with the privileges of the user they are assigned to. Depending on the systems within the network, initializing one of these scripts could apply to more than one or potentially all systems.

entries.name: RC Scripts
entries.text: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system’s startup. These files allow system administrators to map and start custom services at startup for different run levels. RC scripts require root privileges to modify.

entries.name: Startup Items
entries.text: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence. Startup items execute during the final phase of the boot process and contain shell scripts or other executable files along with configuration information used by the system to determine the execution order for all startup items.

entries.name: Data from Network Shared Drive
entries.text: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest. Sensitive data can be collected from remote systems via shared network drives (host shared directory, network file server, etc.) that are accessible from the current system prior to Exfiltration. Interactive command shells may be in use, and common functionality within cmd may be used to gather information.

entries.name: Network Sniffing
entries.text: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network. Network sniffing refers to using the network interface on a system to monitor or capture information sent over a wired or wireless connection.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
entries.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel. Stolen data is encoded into the normal communications channel using the same protocol as command and control communications.

entries.name: Network Service Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation. Common methods to acquire this information include port, vulnerability, and/or wordlist scans using tools that are brought onto a system.

entries.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads. WMI is designed for programmers and is the infrastructure for management data and operations on Windows systems. WMI is an administration feature that provides a uniform environment to access Windows system components.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
entries.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
entries.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
entries.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
entries.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.

entries.name: System Network Connections Discovery
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a physical medium or device introduced by a user. Such media could be an external hard drive, USB drive, cellular phone, MP3 player, or other removable storage and processing device.

entries.name: Exfiltration over USB
entries.text: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a USB device introduced by a user. The USB device could be used as the final exfiltration point or to hop between otherwise disconnected systems.

entries.name: Scheduled Task/Job
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Utilities exist within all major operating systems to schedule programs or scripts to be executed at a specified date and time. A task can also be scheduled on a remote system, provided the proper authentication is met (ex: RPC and file and printer sharing in Windows environments).

entries.name: At
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. The at utility exists as an executable within Windows, Linux, and macOS for scheduling tasks at a specified time and date.

entries.name: Cron
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse the cron utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. The cron utility is a time-based job scheduler for Unix-like operating systems. The crontab file contains the schedule of cron entries to be run and the specified times for execution. Any crontab files are stored in operating system-specific file paths.

entries.name: Scheduled Task
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. There are multiple ways to access the Task Scheduler in Windows. The schtasks utility can be run directly on the command line, or the Task Scheduler can be opened through the GUI within the Administrator Tools section of the Control Panel.

entries.name: Systemd Timers
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse systemd timers to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code. Systemd timers are unit files with file extension .timer that control services. Timers can be set to run on a calendar event or after a time span relative to a starting point. They can be used as an alternative to Cron in Linux environments.

entries.name: Container Orchestration Job
entries.text: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality provided by container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes to schedule deployment of containers configured to execute malicious code. Container orchestration jobs run these automated tasks at a specific date and time, similar to cron jobs on a Linux system.

entries.name: Process Injection
entries.text: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Process injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. Running code in the context of another process may allow access to the process's memory, system/network resources, and possibly elevated privileges.

entries.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
entries.text: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. DLL injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Portable Executable Injection
entries.text: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. PE injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Thread Execution Hijacking
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Thread Execution Hijacking is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Asynchronous Procedure Call
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. APC injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Thread Local Storage
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. TLS callback injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Ptrace System Calls
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via ptrace (process trace) system calls in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Ptrace system call injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Proc Memory
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the /proc filesystem in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Proc memory injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Extra Window Memory Injection
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into a process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. EWM injection is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Process Hollowing
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses. Process hollowing is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: Process Doppelgänging
entries.text: Adversaries may inject malicious code into a process via process doppelgänging in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges. Process doppelgänging is a method of executing arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process.

entries.name: VDSO Hijacking
